caveats: **Configured policy, not effective policy.** Rows are what is written in the policy files, not what the browser enforces. Chromium's own reader is more lenient: it accepts non-strict JSON (this leg reports `linux:json_unparseable`), follows symlinks (this leg refuses them as `linux:symlink_refused`), applies the last file in name order where two files set one policy (this leg reports one row per file with its `source`), and parses every file in a policy directory, not only `*.json`. That last difference is the one direction in which this leg can read as complete while missing a policy: a valid policy file with another name is applied by the browser and skipped here with no constraint reported.

**Windows and macOS are placeholders.** `policies` on those hosts returns one `status` row (`unavailable`) with result status `UNAVAILABLE` and provenance `windows:planned` or `macos:planned`, so a host that was not inspected never reads as having no policy. The Windows registry and macOS Managed Preferences legs are declared but not yet implemented.

**Linux reads machine-level JSON policy files in three vendor directories only.** Only the `managed` and `recommended` `*.json` files under `/etc/opt/chrome`, `/etc/chromium` and `/etc/opt/edge` are read; per-user policy, snap and flatpak Chromium paths, other Chromium-based browsers and Firefox `policies.json` are not, and every row reports scope `machine`. `OK` / `FULL` therefore means those directories were read completely, not that no browser on the host has a policy.

**A file rewritten during the read can be misread for that run.** Each file is read to end after one `fstat` with no second stability check: a file that grows is `linux:oversized` or `linux:json_unparseable`, but a same-size in-place overwrite that lands during the read can parse as a mix of old and new content for that one run, with no token raised. A writer that replaces the file by rename is unaffected, and a run of failing reads is bounded by the per-file (1 MiB) and per-directory (4096 entries) caps rather than the 16 MiB total.

**Values are reported, not validated.** A policy name is emitted as written and is not checked against the browser's schema, so a misspelt policy still appears as a row. Lists and dicts are emitted as compact JSON text, a backslash inside one is folded to `/` and flagged `json_escaped`, and a name, value or source longer than 64 KiB is cut and flagged `truncated`. `value_type` describes how the value is stored in its source, not the browser's schema.

definitions.description: Lists the enterprise-managed Chrome, Chromium and Edge browser policies configured on the device, one row per policy: the browser, whether the policy is mandatory or recommended, its scope, its name, its typed value and the file it was read from. On Linux the rows come from the JSON policy files under /etc/opt/chrome, /etc/chromium and /etc/opt/edge. Windows and macOS legs planned - each follows as its own PR; on those hosts the action returns one `status` row and result status UNAVAILABLE with provenance `<os>:planned`. A host with no managed policy returns zero rows and a clean result status; a read that could not be completed adds a `constrained` status row, followed by one per-path status row naming each file or directory that failed. Values are reported verbatim. The plugin never enforces, fetches or changes anything.

description: Enterprise-managed Chrome, Chromium and Edge browser policy inventory
how_it_works:
`policies` reports which enterprise-managed browser policies an administrator has configured on the device, as facts only. It reads local policy files, in a fixed order: Chrome (`/etc/opt/chrome/policies`), then Chromium (`/etc/chromium/policies`), then Edge (`/etc/opt/edge/policies`), and within each the `managed` directory before `recommended`. Every `*.json` file in those directories is parsed and each top-level key becomes one `policy` row: browser, level (mandatory or recommended), scope, policy name, typed value and the file it came from. Directories are opened one hop at a time without following symlinks, each file is capped at 1 MiB (16 MiB in total per run), and a file that is not a regular file is refused.

The plugin starts no process, uses no network and writes nothing. It enforces and judges nothing: a policy is a row, not a verdict. A missing policy directory means "nothing managed" and produces no rows. A directory or file that exists but cannot be read or decoded makes the result partial and is also written as a `status` row at the top of the output. Only Linux reads policy today; on Windows and macOS the action answers with a single `status` row saying the host was not inspected (see Caveats). The action carries no default-off kill switch because the data is IT-authored configuration, not personal data; the operator-settable per-plugin kill switch still applies.
name: browser_policy

columns.description: Row shape discriminator (field 0): policy (one per configured policy) or status (written first, and only when the read was not complete; the one exception is a leg that throws after it has reported, which appends a second, unavailable status row behind its rows -- the last status row is the outcome). A status row repeats the typed result status in band; its name field is the action, its value field the state and its detail field the reason tokens; its other fields are "-", except source on a per-path status row (the logical path the reason token names).
columns.name: row_kind

columns.description: Browser the policy applies to. Values: chrome (Google Chrome), chromium (Chromium), edge (Microsoft Edge); "-" on a status row.
columns.name: browser

columns.description: Policy level. Values: mandatory (the user cannot override it), recommended (a default the user may change); "-" on a status row.
columns.name: level

columns.description: Where the policy applies. Values: machine, or user:<name> where a leg reads per-user policy (the Linux leg reads machine policy only, so it always reports machine). The user name is untrusted text.
columns.name: scope

columns.description: Policy name exactly as the browser documents it. On a status row: the action name, policies.
columns.name: name

columns.description: Type of the value. Values: bool, int, real, string, list, dict, null, unmodelled (the policy is present but its value could not be represented; see detail); "-" on a status row.
columns.name: value_type

columns.description: The policy value as text: true or false for a bool, decimal text for int and real, the string verbatim, compact JSON text for a list or dict (flagged json_escaped in detail, and lossy and not trustworthy as the original JSON -- an escaped quote can make it syntactically invalid -- if the escaper folded a backslash inside it), the literal null for null, and "-" for unmodelled. Reported verbatim: a value can carry a credential-bearing URL or an enrollment token an administrator put in the file. On a status row: the state, constrained or unavailable.
columns.name: value

columns.description: The logical absolute file the policy was read from, never an injected test root. Only the Linux leg reads policy today; the Windows and macOS legs will report the registry key or plist path. On a status row: "-" on the summary row; on a per-path row the logical /etc/... path of the file or directory whose failure token is in detail, never an injected test root.
columns.name: source

columns.description: A short qualifier, or "-" when there is none. json_type marks an unmodelled value; json_escaped marks a list/dict value whose JSON dump held a backslash, now folded to / by the wire escaper -- the result is lossy and not trustworthy as the original JSON, and an escaped quote can make it syntactically invalid -- the value is still reported, just flagged; nul_replaced and utf8_replaced (appended, comma-joined) mark a free-text field that held an embedded NUL byte or a byte that is not valid UTF-8 (possible in a Linux file name), each replaced by U+FFFD; truncated marks a field longer than 64 KiB, cut. On a status row: the comma-joined reason tokens, for example linux:permission_denied or macos:planned.
columns.name: detail

outputs_note: Every row is pipe-delimited and has nine fields; field 0 is `policy` for a policy row, or `status` for the outcome rows described under Result status. A host with no managed policy returns zero rows. Free text is escaped for the server's pipe grammar (`safe_output_field`, lossy on backslash by design), a field with an embedded NUL byte, or with a byte that is not valid UTF-8 (only a Linux file name can carry one, in `source`), has it replaced by U+FFFD and is flagged in `detail` (`nul_replaced`, `utf8_replaced`), a field longer than 64 KiB is cut and flagged `truncated` (these flags are set on `policy` rows; a `status` row's `source` is repaired and escaped the same way but not flagged, since its `detail` field carries only the reason tokens, repeating the typed status's provenance), and a value that cannot be represented is typed `unmodelled` (`detail` `json_type`) instead of being dropped, and a `list`/`dict` value whose JSON dump contains a backslash — the escaper's fold makes the result lossy and not trustworthy as the original JSON, and an escaped quote in particular can make it syntactically invalid — keeps its type and (folded) text but is flagged `json_escaped` in `detail` rather than presented as trustworthy JSON. `browser_policy` is not in the server's key/value plugin set, so rows are decoded as pipe-separated fields, not as `key|rest`.

privileges.if_refused: n/a - the placeholder reports `UNAVAILABLE` with `windows:planned` and reads nothing
n/a - the placeholder reports `UNAVAILABLE` with `macos:planned` and reads nothing

privileges.grant: None to read - the policy directories are root-owned but must be world-readable for the browser itself to load them
privileges.if_refused: `CONSTRAINED` / partial with a `linux:<detail>` token (for example `linux:permission_denied` or `linux:symlink_refused`); the unreadable directory or file contributes no rows, one `status` row repeats the outcome, and the result never reads as "no policy configured"
privileges.measured: Measured in a Debian 13 container as euid 0 (`docs/samples/linux.txt`: the seeded policy files read with no extra grant); the refusal path (`permission_denied`) is proven by the unit suite as a non-root user, not by a service-account run on a real host
privileges.runs_as: agent daemon, dedicated unprivileged account (`yuzu-agent` on the packaged unit), never root by design (`docs/agent-privilege-model.md`)

result_status.when: Linux: every read completed, populated or genuinely empty; no `status` row

result_status.provenance: `linux:<detail>` with `<detail>` one of `permission_denied`, `symlink_refused`, `not_a_directory`, `open_failed`, `stat_failed`, `not_regular`, `oversized`, `read_failed`, `readdir_error`; also `linux:row_cap` (more than 8192 rows in one run), `linux:entry_cap` (one policy directory holds more than 4096 entries), `linux:byte_cap` (more than 16 MiB of policy files read in one run), `linux:json_unparseable`, `linux:json_not_object`, `linux:json_too_deep` and `linux:json_too_complex` (more than 65536 containers in one file); also `linux:status_rows_capped` (more than 64 per-path `status` rows were due; the first 64 are written) (several tokens are comma-joined)
result_status.when: Linux: a policy directory or file exists but could not be read completely or decoded, or a bound (row cap, directory entry cap, 1 MiB file cap, 16 MiB total parse cap, nesting depth, container count) was hit; a summary `constrained` `status` row plus per-path rows
Windows: the leg is a placeholder; one `unavailable` `status` row, no policy rows
macOS: the leg is a placeholder; one `unavailable` `status` row, no policy rows

result_status.provenance: `windows:leg:exception:<category>` / `macos:leg:exception:<category>` / `linux:leg:exception:<category>`, `<category>` one of `bad_alloc`, `std_exception`, `unknown` (the exception text is deliberately never carried)
result_status.when: a leg threw; reported (with one `unavailable` `status` row) instead of unwinding across the plugin boundary. Under sustained allocation failure the category suffix can be lost, leaving the bare `<os>:leg:exception`, and the row itself may not be written; the typed status (or rc 1) still reaches the host. A leg that throws after it has already reported (an allocation failure while its rows are being written) leaves this `unavailable` row BEHIND the rows already written, after the earlier `constrained` summary and per-path rows: the one case where the status row is neither first nor alone; the last status row and the typed status are the outcome.

stamp.privilege: euid 0 (container seeded with two synthetic Chrome policy files for this capture; see the note under the samples)

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result.** Rows travel over the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response and land in the ResponseStore, queryable at `/api/responses/{id}`. `policies` is also a gathered definition (`crossplatform.browser_policy.policies`, `gather.ttlSeconds` 300: informational, nothing re-dispatches on it).
**Not consumed by** daily-sync, TAR, DEX, or metrics.

**Sensitivity.** Rows are operator/IT-authored configuration: policy names and values such as homepage URLs, allowed or blocked extension ids and proxy settings can disclose part of an organisation's browser-management posture and internal hostnames. They carry no browsing history, bookmarks, cookies or per-user data, and the Linux leg's `scope` column always reports `machine`, never a user. Values are reported verbatim and are not screened: a value an administrator wrote can itself hold a credential-bearing URL or an enrollment token, and the files are world-readable so the browser can load them, so treat the rows as sensitive. Stored responses are kept for the ResponseStore's retention period (90 days by default, `docs/user-manual/response-store.md`); with RBAC on, dispatch needs `Execution:Execute` plus `Inventory:Read` and reading needs `Response:Read`. The classification is deliberate: unlike `browser_inventory`'s per-user browsing data, this content is machine policy the organisation itself wrote, so the action is an ordinary `Inventory:Read` with no execute gate.
**Sibling:** `installed_apps` (which browsers are installed, not how they are managed).
